title: Loaded Baked Potato Bar
seoTitle: Loaded Baked Potato Bar | Firefighter Meal
subtitle: Build-your-own spuds for the crew
description: Build-your-own spuds for the crew. Sized for a full crew, with timing that still works when the kitchen gets interrupted.
equipment: Large cast iron skillet or Dutch oven

steps.title: Scrub and poke potatoes
steps.instruction: Scrub russet potatoes dry. Poke each potato 6–8 times with a fork so steam escapes. Rub skins with vegetable oil and coarse salt — this gives crackly jackets.

steps.title: Bake until fork-tender
steps.instruction: Bake directly on the oven rack at 400°F for 50–65 minutes until a skewer slides in with no resistance. Wrap finished potatoes in foil and hold at 200°F — do not stack hot potatoes or skins go soggy.

steps.title: Prep the topping station
steps.instruction: Line up butter, shredded cheddar, crumbled bacon, sour cream, and green onions in separate bowls with serving spoons. Keep warm toppings near the potatoes; keep sour cream cold on ice if service runs long.

steps.title: Run the potato bar
steps.instruction: Split hot potatoes with a cross-cut and fluff the insides with a fork. Crew builds their own: butter first, then cheddar so it melts, then bacon, sour cream, and green onions. Loaded Baked Potato Bar works best as a self-serve line down the counter.

proTips: Keep a backup tray warm in the oven for late calls — nothing worse than cold plates after a run.
Taste for salt at the end — hall palates run salty after long shifts.
tonightSpread: Label every topping bowl — rookies grab faster when they can read the line.
Keep hot bases (potatoes, chips) in cambros at 200°F and cold toppings on ice if service runs long.
Put forks, napkins, and a trash can at the end of the bar — self-serve feeds get messy fast.
Line up Loaded Baked Potato Bar on the main counter with serving spoons — firefighters grab fast between calls.
Keep a backup tray warm in the oven at 200°F for late arrivals after a run.
leftovers: Cool leftovers in shallow containers within two hours — deep pots stay hot too long.
Label trays with date and reheat to 165°F minimum before second shift.
whyCrewsLikeIt: Build-your-own spuds for the crew. A hall pick for regular dinner nights — one line, real portions, no drama at the stove.
